title: ₹130 Crore and Half of Bollywood: Riteish Deshmukh's Raja Shivaji Just Landed on Netflix
excerpt: The highest-grossing Marathi film of all time — with Sanjay Dutt, Abhishek Bachchan, Vidya Balan, and a Salman Khan cameo — is now streaming in Hindi and Marathi. Diaspora, this is your moment.
body:
There are debuts, and then there are coronations. When **Riteish Deshmukh** stepped behind the camera and into the armour of **Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj** for *Raja Shivaji*, he wasn't just making a movie — he was cashing in a decade-long promise to himself, to Marathi cinema, and to a warrior-king whose story has waited far too long for the screen it deserves.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=IeP5Zl0C-hw</youtube>

And now, after a six-week theatrical run that rewrote every record in Marathi cinema's ledger, the film is finally streaming. **Netflix dropped Raja Shivaji on June 26 in both Hindi and Marathi** — which means if you're sitting in New Jersey or Leicester or Brampton and missed it in theatres, your weekend plans just changed.

## The Numbers That Rewrite the Record Books

Let's talk scale. *Raja Shivaji* opened on Maharashtra Day — May 1 — and didn't slow down. ₹11.35 crore on opening day. ₹43.66 crore in its first weekend. By Day 17, it had crossed **Sairat**'s legendary lifetime to become the highest-grossing Marathi film at the domestic box office. By Day 18, it became the first Marathi film ever to hit ₹100 crore net. Its worldwide theatrical haul settled at **₹130 crore** — staggering for a Marathi-language production, even one made on the ₹75-crore budget that made it the most expensive Marathi film ever produced.

The Hindi version alone pulled in approximately ₹29 crore gross, drawing audiences from urban multiplex circuits well beyond Maharashtra. This isn't a regional film anymore. It's a crossover event.

## The Cast That Showed Up for a King

Look at this lineup and tell me it doesn't read like an awards-night seating chart. **Sanjay Dutt** as the menacing Afzal Khan. **Abhishek Bachchan** as Sambhaji Shahaji Bhosale. **Vidya Balan** as Khadija Sultana — a role originally offered to Tabu, who had to pass due to scheduling conflicts with *Bhooth Bangla*. **Fardeen Khan** as Shah Jahan. **Bhagyashree** as Rajmata Jijabai. **Mahesh Manjrekar**, **Sachin Khedekar**, **Boman Irani**, **Jitendra Joshi** — every one of them serving performances worthy of the period regalia.

And then there's the cameo everyone still talks about: **Salman Khan** as Jiva Mahale, the warrior who saved Shivaji's life during the ambush by Afzal Khan's lieutenant. Khan filmed his portions across two intense days in November 2025, and if you know his Marathi-cinema track record — *Lai Bhaari*, *Ved* — you know he shows up for Riteish like few others.

Behind the lens, **Santosh Sivan** — yes, *that* Santosh Sivan, the man behind *Dil Se* and *Iruvar* — shot the Sahyadri mountains and fort landscapes like they were characters in their own right. **Ajay-Atul** delivered a soundtrack anchored by the thunderous "Chhatrapati" anthem that became a cultural event in its own right. Even Riteish's sons Riaan and Rahyl stepped in to play younger versions of Shivaji, making this the most personal film of Deshmukh's career.

## What the Critics Said — and What Audiences Decided

The reviews were respectful, if not rapturous. *Bollywood Hungama* gave it 4 stars, calling it "a fine ode to one of India's greatest kings." *News18* praised Deshmukh's "controlled performance and steady direction." *Filmfare* noted the film delivered "a dignified murmur" where the story demanded "a roar." Others pointed to uneven VFX, a 195-minute runtime that tested patience, and a conventional good-versus-evil framing that kept Shivaji as icon rather than man.

But here's the thing: audiences didn't care about the critical qualifications. They packed theatres across Maharashtra and beyond, returned for second viewings, and turned this into a genuine cultural moment — the kind where the Bombay High Court had to dismiss a PIL objecting to the film's title just two days before release. The court called it "motivated." Maharashtrians called it *their* film.

## Why the Diaspora Should Stream This Weekend

*Raja Shivaji* isn't just streaming now — it's streaming in **Hindi**, which matters enormously for NRIs who grew up hearing about Shivaji Maharaj at home but never had access to a theatrical Marathi blockbuster of this scale. Netflix's global footprint means this film is now available in every city where there's a Maharashtrian living room and a Wi-Fi connection.

The film covers Shivaji's journey before his coronation as Chhatrapati in 1674 — his childhood under Jijabai's fierce guidance, his guerrilla warfare tactics against the Adil Shahi Sultanate and Mughal forces, the building of a loyal army, and the famous confrontation with Afzal Khan that serves as the film's electrifying climax. It's structured in eight chapters, each a discrete historical moment, each staged with the sweep and colour of an Amar Chitra Katha panel come to roaring life.

Is it perfect? No. Is it important? Absolutely. And for Riteish Deshmukh — a man who first announced this project in 2015 and spent eleven years willing it into existence — it's something closer to a life's work.
